2026-08-04.headline: Note: 4 Aug figures are intraday prints; the last confirmed close is Monday 3 Aug. The integrity check clears — the 3 Aug row has refreshed with true closes, and four series that were dark in the last edition have backfilled. Score RISES to 27/30 — political stress fires 4→5 on the two-close rule, the highest reading since 31 May and the first upgrade since 31 July. The trigger fired on a backfill rather than on a new print: AUTMUSAG, the scored AAA pump series, was blank for 31 July when the last edition went out, and the extract has now filled it at $4.76 — a second consecutive confirmed close above the $4.75 threshold after the $4.76 of 30 July. That is the sustained break the rule requires, and it is the same mechanism that fired US inflation on 31 July. The second development runs the other way and cancels yesterday's optimism. The talks announced for 3 August did not convene. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said flatly on Monday that 'we are not negotiating with the United States at this time'; US officials told CBS News that no new negotiations are planned, contradicting the President, who said the same day that talks were under way 'at the request of Iran' and called it Iran's 'last chance' before what he termed decapitation. No venue, no attendee list, no readout and no Omani confirmation could be sourced from any outlet. The escalation downgrade candidate that this monitor carried for one edition is therefore revoked, not merely deferred — which is precisely why hysteresis governs event channels as well as market channels. Baghaei also said the strait 'will in no way return to the status it was before February 28th', a line this monitor could not corroborate last week under a different attribution and can now source at Tier 1. Third, the dated supply test landed and it landed hard: Treasury raised its July–September net marketable borrowing estimate to $739bn from the $671bn projected on 4 May, an increase of $68bn, with the refunding statement due Wednesday and the 30Y leg the week of 10 August, into a long end 17.74 bp above the May auction stop. Crude did not follow the diplomacy back up: Brent front-month prints $81.92, up $0.83 but still $0.16 below last Tuesday. Five of six channels are now maxed. Only oil, at 2/5, can raise this number further. Sequencing 26 → 26 → 27.

THE ANNOUNCED 3 AUGUST TALKS DID NOT CONVENE — THE TWO GOVERNMENTS NOW CONTRADICT EACH OTHER

No outlet could source a session, a venue, an attendee list, a readout or an Omani confirmation. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at his Monday press conference: ‘We are not negotiating with the United States at this time,’ adding that the Iranian delegation ‘is not going anywhere, and is not expecting anyone to visit’; Foreign Minister Araghchi was in Iraq for Arbaeen. US officials separately told CBS News that no new negotiations with Iran are planned. President Trump said the same day that ‘we’re talking, and we’re talking at the request of Iran, backed by Saudi Arabia, backed by UAE and backed by Qatar,’ called it ‘a last chance for them to sign a good document’, said he was under no time constraint, and said he wanted to give Iran ‘every last chance before decapitation.’ He also said the strait could be ‘open literally by tomorrow, completely open.’
CBS News / Euronews / The National / ABC News / CNN / Bloomberg / The Hill
Iran hardens the terms: the strait ‘will in no way return’ to its pre-war status

Baghaei said the Strait ‘will in no way return to the status it was before February 28th’; that the Oman track concerns a TEMPORARY route and is ‘a necessary but not sufficient condition’ for reopening; and that reopening requires mechanisms protecting Iranian sovereignty. ABC News describes the concept as a single transit corridor replacing the divided northern and southern routes, with the toll — who levies it and at what rate — still disputed. Note: the 31 Jul edition attributed a similar line to Gharibabadi and the 3 Aug edition withdrew it as uncorroborated; it is now sourced at Tier 1 to Baghaei on 3 Aug and is used on that basis. No Iran–Oman corridor agreement has been signed; the only instrument on record is the 23 Jun joint statement establishing a working group.
The National / ABC News / Oman Ministry of Foreign Affairs
No new confirmed strike, but the strike option is documented and on the table

CENTCOM has issued no strike release since 29 Jul, and no Tier 1 outlet reported a new US or Israeli strike on Iran on 3 or 4 Aug. The planning is now corroborated beyond a single outlet: CBS News reported on 31 Jul that the US and Israel were preparing strikes on Iranian power plants and refineries, potentially including electricity systems across Tehran, with Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell on the record that the department is ‘locked and loaded, ready to execute the President’s directives’ and the President yet to give final go orders. The ‘roughly two-week campaign’ duration carried in earlier editions is NOT corroborated — CBS describes a weekend-scale window. UKMTO’s report of an explosion beside a tanker about 20 nm north-east of Khasab appears in Gulf outlets dated 3 Aug with the same particulars as the 2 Aug report; it is treated as ONE incident, not two.
CENTCOM / CBS News / The Hill / Jerusalem Post / Sharjah24 / UKMTO
Treasury raises Q3 borrowing by $68bn; OPEC+ delivers September barrels

The US Treasury said on 3 Aug it expects to borrow $739bn of net marketable debt in July–September, $68bn above the $671bn projected on 4 May, and $628bn in October–December, assuming cash balances of $950bn at end-September and $850bn at end-December; excluding a higher starting balance the underlying increase is $87bn. The refunding statement follows on Wednesday 5 Aug. On the physical side, the OPEC+ eight confirmed the September increase of 188k b/d with a country split (Saudi +62k, Russia +62k, Iraq +26k, Kuwait +16k, Kazakhstan +10k, Algeria +6k, Oman +5k); the 67th JMMC of 2 Aug ‘emphasised the importance of protecting maritime routes and energy infrastructure from attacks.’ Aramco’s 400k b/d Jizan complex is targeted to restart about 15 Aug; Abqaiq and Damietta remain unreported since late July. ISM manufacturing for July came in at 55.6 against 54.0 expected, with the prices index easing to 71.1.

analysis.intro: The shock rises to 27/30 on a single channel move, and the move came from a backfill rather than from a new print. AUTMUSAG, the AAA pump series that carries political stress, was blank for 31 July when the last edition was written; this extract fills it at $4.76, a second consecutive confirmed close above the $4.75 trigger, and the channel fires 4→5 on exactly the two-close rule that fired US inflation on 31 July. Everything else in the market tape was quiet: Monday’s closes came in within a basis point or two of the Singapore-morning snapshot across the curve, Brent closed 47 cents below its morning print, and Tuesday’s intraday range in Brent is 74 cents. The news, by contrast, was not quiet. The negotiations announced for Monday did not take place; Iran’s foreign ministry said on the record that it is not negotiating with the United States; US officials told CBS that no talks are planned; and the President said talks were under way and described the alternative as decapitation. That is not an ambiguous readout, it is an absence of one, and the escalation downgrade candidate opened last edition is closed. Against that, the dated supply test arrived: Treasury raised its Q3 borrowing estimate by $68bn into a long end sitting 17.74 bp above the May auction stop, with the refunding statement tomorrow.
analysis.bondYieldNote: 4 Aug yields are intraday; the 3 Aug close is confirmed and every trigger runs off it. One channel moved: political stress 4→5. Score rises to 27/30.

bondYield.title: (i) Political stress — UPGRADED 4→5, the trigger fired by a backfill.
bondYield.text: This is the move of the edition and it needs to be stated precisely, because it was decided by data that arrived rather than by data that changed. AUTMUSAG printed exactly $4.75 on 24, 27, 28 and 29 July, then $4.76 on 30 July — its first reading through the $4.75 threshold and its highest since 10 June. On 31 July the series went blank and the 3 August edition held the channel at 4, ARMED, because one close above a trigger is not a sustained break. This extract has backfilled 31 July at $4.76. That is a second consecutive confirmed close above the trigger, which is the definition of a sustained break this monitor has applied consistently — it is the identical construction that fired US inflation 4→5 on 31 July after two consecutive closes above 2.20%, and the discipline that stopped the oil channel whipsawing on 25–26 June. The channel therefore moves to 5/5 and the score to 27/30. Two qualifications belong with it. First, the series is blank again for 3 and 4 August, so the upgrade rests on 30 and 31 July and not on anything more recent. Second, the corroborating retail series is stalling rather than accelerating: GasBuddy’s national average was $4.05 on 3 August, down 0.8 cents on the week. What is NOT stalling is diesel — GasBuddy has it up 7.1 cents on the week to $5.326 and EIA had on-highway diesel up 17.9 cents in the week to 27 July against gasoline’s 9.5. The pass-through constraint remains refining rather than crude, which is why Brent at $81 does not disarm this channel. No federal intervention — SPR release, export limit, waiver or gouging action — is confirmable in the window.

bondYield.title: (ii) Escalation risk — held at 5 (max), and the downgrade candidate is REVOKED rather than deferred.
bondYield.text: The 3 August edition opened the first live downgrade candidate this channel has had since 9 July, on the strength of a cancelled US strike package and an announced negotiation, and deliberately did not take it because an announcement is not a stand-down. That judgment is now vindicated by the outcome rather than by the reasoning. The talks did not convene. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman said on the record that Tehran is not negotiating with Washington and that its delegation is going nowhere; the foreign minister was in Iraq; US officials told CBS News that no negotiations are planned; and no outlet could source a venue, an attendee list, a readout, or a confirmation from Oman. The President’s own account — that talks were under way at Iran’s request — is contradicted by his own officials and by Tehran simultaneously, and he paired it with an explicit threat of decapitation. Two further facts push the same way. CBS News independently corroborated the reporting that the US and Israel are preparing strikes on Iranian power plants and refineries, with a named Pentagon spokesman on the record that the department is ‘locked and loaded’ and only the final order outstanding — so what was a single-outlet Al Jazeera item is now a multi-outlet one, though the ‘two-week campaign’ duration is not corroborated. And Iran hardened its terms: Baghaei said the strait ‘will in no way return to the status it was before February 28th’ and that an Oman route deal is necessary but not sufficient to reopen it. The channel stays pinned at its maximum and the path to a downgrade is now longer than it was 24 hours ago.

bondYield.title: (iii) Treasury — held at 5 (max), and the supply test has arrived.
bondYield.text: The 30Y closed 5.2274% on 3 August and the 10Y 4.6755%, keeping both Stage-4 legs satisfied on a fourth consecutive close; this morning’s 5.2327% and 4.6858% carry them to a fifth session. Both downgrade legs continue to fail: the 30Y is 22.74 bp above the 5.00% line on the close, and MOVE at 80.48 is 5.48 pts above the 75 leg even after giving back 2.54 from Friday’s spike. The material development is fiscal, not monetary. Treasury said on Monday it now expects to borrow $739bn of net marketable debt in July–September, $68bn more than the $671bn it projected on 4 May, and $628bn in October–December, on assumed cash balances of $950bn at end-September and $850bn at end-December; Reuters reports that stripping out a higher-than-assumed starting balance leaves an underlying increase of $87bn, attributed to lower projected cash flows. The second quarter closed with $190bn borrowed and a $919bn cash balance, $1bn above plan. The refunding statement follows at 8:30am ET on Wednesday 5 August against 6 May guidance holding coupon sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn ‘for at least the next several quarters’, and the 30Y leg auctions in the week of 10 August. A long end 17.74 bp above the May auction stop now has a quantified increase in supply to absorb, and the question the auction answers is no longer hypothetical.

bondYield.title: (iv) US inflation impulse — held at 5 (max), and still not fading.
bondYield.text: 5Y5Y forward inflation closed at 2.3376% on 3 August, a fifth consecutive close above the 2.30% trigger, and prints the identical 2.3376% this morning. The series has now run 2.3302%, 2.3303%, 2.3597%, 2.3376% and 2.3376% across five sessions; it gave back 2.21 bp from the war record and no more. The 10Y breakeven has behaved differently and the difference is informative: after closing 2.2846% on 31 July, its highest since 3 July, it closed 2.2622% on Monday and prints 2.2603% now, back to within a third of a basis point of its 2.2569% pre-war anchor. Near-term compensation has normalised while the forward has not, which is the signature of a market pricing a persistent policy-credibility problem rather than a transitory energy shock — and it is worth noting that this happened while Brent fell nearly $7 on Monday and the ISM prices index eased to 71.1 from 73.0. The downgrade, 5Y5Y sustained at or below the 2.142% anchor, is 19.56 bp away and not in play. At 5/5 the channel can only subtract.

bondYield.title: (v) Oil — held at 2, and this is the only channel left that can raise the score.
bondYield.text: The last confirmed close is $81.09 (3 August), $13.91 below the $95 upgrade trigger and $8.61 above the $72.48 downgrade anchor — the narrowest that downgrade gap has been since 10 July. This morning Brent prints $81.92, up $0.83, in a 74-cent range. What is notable is what did not happen: the diplomacy that took $6.84 out of Brent on Monday turned out not to exist, and Brent recovered 83 cents. The $6.44 Brent–WTI spread that collapsed to $3.14 on the announcement has stayed near $3. The market has priced the OPEC+ September increment and the removal of the immediate strike risk, and has not re-priced the failure of the talks. The physical case for a higher number is unchanged and arguably firmer: effective OPEC+ spare capacity was roughly 0.17 mb/d on the IEA’s July estimate, so September’s 188k b/d is a quota rather than a cargo; Jizan’s 400k b/d is out to about 15 August; Abqaiq still shows unexplained burn scars; Damietta’s status since the 29–30 July strike is still unreported; and the strait is closed on day 156 with route-undetermined traffic at roughly 41% of crossings. The channel stays at 2 because $81.09 is not $95. But with five of six channels now maxed, oil is the only one that can move this score up, and the downgrade leg it acquired last edition — a mediated pause — has just been withdrawn.

bondYield.title: (vi) Maritime denial — held at 5 (max).
bondYield.text: The strait is closed on day 156 and Iran has now stated at Tier 1 that it will not return to its pre-war status. Kpler’s all-crossings series shows the week to 2 August at 106 crossings by 96 vessels against 98 the week before, an 8% rise, with route-undetermined traffic easing from about 49% to about 41%; that is a marginal improvement from a crisis baseline and nothing like the 25%-of-normal-for-ten-sessions the downgrade requires. Windward logged 19 crossings on 1 August with 6 dark, against roughly 140 a day pre-crisis, and 1,130 GPS-jammed vessels in the Gulf, up 173% on its seven-day average. No corridor agreement has been signed; the only instrument on record remains the 23 June Oman–Iran joint statement establishing a working group.

analysis.stage4Note: Stage 4 is a credit/auction event. Threshold B is satisfied on four consecutive confirmed closes and the supply number is now published rather than assumed.

stage4.title: Threshold A · 13 May 30Y auction, cleared 5.050% — the test is now quantified.
stage4.text: Historical benchmark; the 9 July re-opening cleared 5.06% with a 0.3 bp stop-through. The 3 August close of 5.2274% is 17.74 bp above the May stop, narrower than Friday’s war-widest 22.24 bp but still the second-widest week of the war. On Monday Treasury published the number this monitor has been waiting for: net marketable borrowing of $739bn for July–September against the $671bn projected on 4 May, an increase of $68bn, with $628bn guided for October–December and assumed cash balances of $950bn at end-September and $850bn at end-December. Reuters attributes the rise to lower projected cash flows only partly offset by a higher starting balance, and puts the underlying increase at $87bn. April–June closed with $190bn borrowed and a $919bn end-June balance, $1bn above the May assumption. The refunding statement lands at 8:30am ET on Wednesday 5 August; the 6 May guidance held coupon auction sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn and promised no increase ‘for at least the next several quarters.’ If that guidance survives a $68bn upgrade to the quarter’s borrowing need, the bill market absorbs it; if it does not, the 30Y leg in the week of 10 August is the first coupon auction of a larger programme into a long end already at war highs. That is the specific sequence that would make Threshold A live rather than historical.

stage4.title: Threshold B · 30Y above 5.20% with 10Y above 4.65% — SATISFIED on four consecutive confirmed closes.
stage4.text: 29 July: 5.2007% / 4.6773%. 30 July: 5.2135% / 4.6733%. 31 July: 5.2724% / 4.7347%, both war records. 3 August: 5.2274% / 4.6755%. Monday cleared the legs by 2.74 bp and 2.55 bp, against 7.24 bp and 8.47 bp on Friday — a narrower but still unambiguous pass, and the point of a persistence threshold is persistence rather than margin. This morning’s 5.2327% and 4.6858% keep both satisfied on a fifth session. The qualification is unchanged: the threshold warns that the long end is repricing in a way that historically precedes an auction or credit event; it is not a Stage-4 event in itself. What has changed is that the event it warns about now has a date and a size. The mechanism arming it remains domestic fiscal and monetary credibility rather than a Hormuz headline — which is why a failed negotiation moved crude 83 cents and moved the 30Y half a basis point.

stage4.title: Threshold C · MOVE above 130. Far off, and it eased this session.
stage4.text: The index closed at 80.48 on 3 August, down 2.54 from Friday’s 83.02, its highest since 19 May. That leaves 49.52 pts to the threshold and it remains well under the 115.02 war high of 26 March, so C is not close. Two observations belong with it anyway. First, at 80.48 the index is still 5.48 pts above the 75 line that forms the second leg of the Treasury downgrade, so the same reading that keeps C remote keeps that downgrade unavailable. Second, a fall in rates volatility on the session before a refunding statement is not obviously reassurance; it is the market declining to pre-position. There is no 4 August print, and the number is flagged rather than carried as fresh.

analysis.crossAsset: The cross-asset signature this session is stillness in the market and rupture in the news, which is close to the inverse of Friday. Monday’s closes landed within two basis points of the Singapore-morning snapshot everywhere on the curve: the 30Y at 5.2274% against 5.2370% published, the 10Y at 4.6755% against 4.6939%, 5Y5Y at 2.3376% against 2.3367%. MOVE eased 2.54 to 80.48, VIX 0.13 to 15.86 and its lowest since 10 July, and the dollar firmed back above 100 for the first time since 29 July. Brent closed $81.09, 47 cents below its morning print, and this morning trades in a 74-cent range at $81.92 — a market with nothing to price. Yet in the same 24 hours the announced US–Iran negotiation failed to materialise and the two governments issued mutually exclusive accounts of whether it exists, Iran stated that the strait will not return to its pre-war status, and the US Treasury told the market it needs to borrow $68bn more this quarter than it said in May. Equity and rates volatility both fell through that. Henry Hub at $2.768 remains 9.6% BELOW pre-war, so the routing signature is intact and this is still not a global-energy shock. The reading to take is not that the news stopped mattering; it is that the market has stopped trading Hormuz headlines and started waiting for Wednesday.

items: Score rises to 27/30 on the political-stress upgrade. The announced talks did not convene. Treasury raises Q3 borrowing by $68bn. Four dark series backfill. Source: Bloomberg unless stated.

AUTMUSAG backfilled 31 July at $4.76 — the second consecutive close through the political trigger, and the channel fires 4→5. The scored AAA pump series printed exactly $4.75 on 24, 27, 28 and 29 July, $4.76 on 30 July — its first reading through the $4.75 threshold and its highest since 10 June — and was blank for 31 July when the last edition went out. This extract fills 31 July at $4.76. Two consecutive confirmed closes above a trigger is the sustained break the rule requires, and it is the same construction that fired US inflation 4→5 on 31 July. Political stress moves to 5/5 and the score to 27/30. Source: Bloomberg.

The talks announced for 3 August did not convene, and the two governments now contradict each other in public. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told his Monday press conference: ‘We are not negotiating with the United States at this time,’ adding that Iran’s delegation ‘is not going anywhere, and is not expecting anyone to visit’; Foreign Minister Araghchi was in Iraq for Arbaeen. US officials told CBS News that no new negotiations are planned. President Trump said the same day that talks were under way ‘at the request of Iran, backed by Saudi Arabia, backed by UAE and backed by Qatar’, called it ‘a last chance for them to sign a good document’ and said he wanted to give Iran ‘every last chance before decapitation’. No venue, attendee list, readout or Omani confirmation could be sourced. Source: CBS News / The National / Euronews / ABC News / CNN / The Hill.

The escalation downgrade candidate is revoked — the first time this monitor has opened and closed one in consecutive editions. The 3 August edition opened the channel’s first live downgrade since 9 July and deliberately did not take it, on the ground that an announcement is not a stand-down. The talks did not happen. Had the channel been moved on the announcement, it would have had to be reversed within a session — the 25–26 June error repeated in the opposite direction. The rule that prevented it is recorded in section 9. Source: as above.

Treasury raised its July–September borrowing estimate to $739bn, $68bn above the May projection. The estimate published Monday 3 August puts net marketable borrowing at $739bn for July–September against the $671bn projected on 4 May, and $628bn for October–December, assuming cash balances of $950bn at end-September and $850bn at end-December. Reuters attributes the increase to lower projected cash flows only partly offset by a higher starting balance and puts the underlying rise at $87bn. April–June closed with $190bn borrowed and a $919bn end-June balance. The refunding statement follows at 8:30am ET on Wednesday 5 August; the 30Y leg auctions the week of 10 August. Source: Reuters / MT Newswires / US Treasury.

Iran hardened its terms on the strait, and the line this monitor withdrew last week is now sourceable at Tier 1. Baghaei said on 3 August that the Strait ‘will in no way return to the status it was before February 28th’, that the Oman track concerns a temporary route and is ‘a necessary but not sufficient condition’ for reopening, and that reopening requires mechanisms protecting Iranian sovereignty. The 31 July edition attributed a similar line to Gharibabadi and the 3 August edition withdrew it as uncorroborated; it is restored here on a Tier 1 attribution to Baghaei. ABC News describes the corridor concept as a single transit route replacing the divided northern and southern corridors, with the toll still disputed. Source: The National / ABC News.

Four dark series backfilled — and one of them decided the score. The 3 August edition flagged JGLA, AUTMUSAG and SOFR as running dark, with MOVE and VIX carried as Friday closes. This extract fills AUTMUSAG for 31 July at $4.76, SOFR for 31 July at 3.66, JGLA for 3 August at ¥3,421, and MOVE and VIX for 3 August at 80.48 and 15.86. AUTMUSAG and SOFR remain blank for 3 and 4 August and JGLA for 4 August. This is the second consecutive month in which a §9.8-flagged blackout has resolved on backfill within two sessions. Source: Bloomberg.

The strike option is corroborated beyond a single outlet, with the Pentagon on the record. CBS News reported on 31 July that the US and Israel were preparing strikes on Iranian power plants and refineries, potentially including electricity systems across Tehran, with Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell stating the department is ‘locked and loaded, ready to execute the President’s directives’ and the President yet to give final go orders. The Hill and the Jerusalem Post carried the same reporting. The ‘roughly two-week campaign’ duration carried in earlier editions is NOT corroborated — CBS describes a weekend-scale window — and that qualifier is corrected here. Source: CBS News / The Hill / Jerusalem Post.

Correction: the Iraqi militia deadline is corroborated above Tier 3, and there are two dates, not one. The 3 August edition demoted this item to Tier 3. Rudaw reported on 29 July that the Islamic Resistance in Iraq set 7 August for Iraqi government bodies to act on disarmament demands, with any response deferred until after Arbaeen; Ynetnews reported the same day that Kataib Hezbollah gave Baghdad until 6 August. Both are above Tier 3 and appear to be related but distinct ultimatums. The trigger event is confirmed: US–Saudi strikes on Popular Mobilization Forces in Diyala killed 20 including Iranian advisers, and CENTCOM issued a release on 28 July. Source: Rudaw / Ynetnews / CENTCOM.

Monday’s reconciliation was the smallest in a fortnight — the opposite of Friday’s record gap. The 3 August close came in within two basis points of the Singapore-morning snapshot across the curve and 47 cents below it in Brent. Friday’s gaps were $1.97 and 7.59 bp. The lesson is not that the snapshot is reliable but that its error is regime-dependent: it is large when the US session has news to trade and small when it does not. Source: Bloomberg.

OPEC+ published the September country split; ISM manufacturing beat; the EIA weekly is still to come. The 188k b/d September increase breaks down as Saudi +62k, Russia +62k, Iraq +26k, Kuwait +16k, Kazakhstan +10k, Algeria +6k, Oman +5k; the 67th JMMC of 2 August emphasised ‘protecting maritime routes and energy infrastructure from attacks’ and the next meetings are 6 September and 4 October. ISM manufacturing for July printed 55.6 against 54.0 expected, with production at 58.5 (highest since November 2021), employment at 52.8 (first expansion in 33 months) and prices easing to 71.1. No new EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report has been released — the next is due 5 August, and the 24 July print stands with SPR at 307.7 mb after a 3.7 mb draw. Source: Rigzone / OPEC / ISM / EIA.

What survives is the bilateral Iran–Oman corridor negotiation, which Araghchi called near-final on 2 Aug and which Baghaei on 3 Aug described as temporary, sovereignty-conditioned and ‘necessary but not sufficient’. The stated objectives remain incompatible — ‘immediate, complete and total opening’ against a strait that ‘will in no way return’ to its pre-war status.

The negotiation did not happen and Iran denies one is under way. What remains is the Oman corridor track, which is about managing a closed strait rather than ending a war.

2026-08-04.scenarioShift: Probability shifts from the 3 Aug edition: mediated pause −7 (12→5), the largest single fall in the map, because the announced talks did not convene and Iran’s foreign ministry stated on the record that it is not negotiating with Washington; full war +6 (34→40) and modal again, on the failed negotiation, the ‘decapitation’ framing and CBS’s corroboration of strike planning against Iranian power plants and refineries with the Pentagon ‘locked and loaded’; contained-but-violent +1 (15→16), the path the tape is actually pricing; regional relapse +1 (12→13) on unchanged exposure and two pending Iraqi militia deadlines; deal collapse −1 (27→26), lower only because part of it has already happened. Probabilities sum to 100.
watchlist: The refunding statement, Wednesday 5 August at 8:30am ET — the single most consequential scheduled event on the calendar. Treasury raised its July–September net marketable borrowing estimate to $739bn on Monday, $68bn above the 4 May projection of $671bn, with $628bn guided for October–December. The 6 May refunding held coupon sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn and promised no increase ‘for at least the next several quarters.’ Whether that guidance survives the upgrade is the question. The 30Y refunding leg auctions in the week of 10 August into a long end that closed 17.74 bp above the 13 May auction stop and has satisfied Stage-4 Threshold B on four consecutive closes.

AUTMUSAG’s next print — the upgrade has fired, so the question is now whether it holds. The channel moved on 30 and 31 July at $4.76. The series is blank for 3 and 4 August. A backfill materially below $4.75 would not reverse the upgrade (hysteresis requires a sustained reversal past a wider threshold) but it would change the read on how durable the break is. Watch GasBuddy alongside it: its national average fell 0.8 cents on the week to $4.05 on 3 August while diesel rose 7.1 cents to $5.326, and Patrick De Haan attributes the product strength to Ukrainian strikes on Russian refining rather than to Hormuz.

Whether any US–Iran session actually takes place, and whether Oman confirms it. The escalation downgrade is now further away than it was, and reopening it requires more than another announcement: a session that demonstrably convened, mediator confirmation, an end to Tehran’s public denial that talks exist, and no new strike, sustained across several sessions. Note the asymmetry — CENTCOM has issued no strike release since 29 July, so the absence of strikes is real; it is the presence of a negotiation that cannot be sourced.

The EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, Wednesday 5 August — and the SPR line in particular. No weekly has been released since the 29 July print for the week to 24 July: crude 404.5 mb and about 6% below the five-year average, gasoline 211.3 mb and 7% below, distillate about 10% below, refinery utilisation 97.2%, and SPR 307.7 mb after a 3.7 mb draw. Refinery utilisation at 97.2% with distillate 10% below average is the mechanism that keeps the political channel elevated independent of crude.

July payrolls on 7 August and July CPI on 12 August, into a market pricing a September HIKE. The FOMC held on 29 July at 3.50–3.75% by 9–3 with all three dissents FOR a hike. Polymarket had roughly 60% on a 25 bp September hike as of 2 August; no live CME FedWatch reading for 3–4 August could be sourced. Payrolls consensus is around +88k with unemployment at 4.2%. JOLTS for June is due today. Both prints land before the 15–16 September meeting, and 5Y5Y at 2.3376% says the market does not believe the inflation argument has been won.

The 6 and 7 August Iraqi militia deadlines, and three series to re-verify. Ynetnews reported Kataib Hezbollah giving Baghdad until 6 August; Rudaw reported the Islamic Resistance in Iraq setting 7 August, with any response deferred until after Arbaeen. Both are above Tier 3 and both follow the 28–29 July US–Saudi strikes in Diyala. On the data side: JGLA has no 4 August print and is never carried forward; AUTMUSAG and SOFR are blank for 3 and 4 August; MOVE and VIX printed for 3 August but not 4 August.

methodology.scale: Six transmission channels (maritime denial, oil, US inflation impulse, Treasury stress, political stress, escalation risk), each 0–5, summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch · 8–14 stress · 15–21 systemic-risk watch · 22–30 crisis. Market channels move only on a confirmed close through a trigger; escalation-risk and maritime denial are event-based. Hysteresis: upgrades fire on a sustained break, downgrades only on a sustained reversal past a wider threshold, deliberately, to avoid whipsawing. This edition is the clearest vindication of that rule the monitor has produced. On the upgrade side, political stress held at 4 on 3 August with one close above its trigger and fires today only because a second consecutive close arrived — the identical two-close construction that fired US inflation on 31 July. On the downgrade side, the escalation channel was NOT moved on 3 August despite a cancelled strike package and an announced negotiation, on the stated ground that an announcement is not a stand-down; the negotiation then did not take place, and a channel moved on that evidence would have had to be reversed within a single session — the 25–26 June error, repeated in the opposite direction. Event channels are governed by hysteresis exactly as market channels are.
methodology.scaleCap: Maritime and escalation have been pinned at 5/5 since 10 and 9 July, Treasury since 14 July, US inflation since 31 July, and political stress joins them today. Only oil, at 2/5, retains any upward range — three points in a thirty-point scale. Two consequences follow and readers should hold both. First, further geopolitical deterioration cannot raise this score; if the strike package that CBS reports as awaiting authorisation is executed, the number moves only if Brent closes above $95. Second, the cap also hides improvement: a genuine de-escalation would not lower the score until it had persisted long enough to move an event channel off its maximum. A flat 27 from here should be read as a saturated scale, not as a stable situation.

Score HOLDS at 27/30. No channel moved. Two things happened, and they run in opposite directions. First, the market took the war premium out with both hands. Brent closed $77.93 on Tuesday, $3.16 below Monday and $10.00 below Friday’s close — the largest two-session fall since 6 May and the lowest close since 10 July, and it did so alongside a 6.3 bp fall in the 10Y close and 5.3 bp in the 30Y. Second, and this is why nothing moved, the diplomacy this monitor could not source yesterday has acquired a real and differently-constituted form. Iran now publicly confirms a negotiation — but with Oman, not with Washington. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Tuesday that Tehran is in bilateral talks with Muscat on safe inbound and outbound shipping lanes; Secretary of State Rubio said there had been ‘progress made in those talks, but not finality yet’; and Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC ‘there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait.’ Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman said in the same 24 hours that no direct US–Iran talks are scheduled. analysis.intro: The shock holds at 27/30 and no channel moved, but the composition of the risk changed more in this session than in the last three combined. The market de-risked hard: Brent’s 4 August close of $77.93 is $10.00 below Friday’s, the largest two-session fall since 6 May, and the entire Treasury curve closed 5.8 to 7.3 bp below the Singapore-morning snapshot. That has a mechanical consequence — Stage-4 Threshold B, satisfied on four consecutive closes including two war records, is no longer satisfied — and a directional one: the oil channel’s downgrade anchor is now $5.45 away, closer than at any point since 10 July. The news moved the other way in form but the same way in substance. The negotiation this monitor could not source on Monday exists after all, but it is an Iran–Oman corridor negotiation that Tehran confirms and a US–Iran negotiation that Qatar and Tehran both deny. That is a materially better-evidenced diplomatic track than the one revoked yesterday, and it is the first credible route to a MARITIME downgrade rather than an escalation one. It is not a stand-down: a bulk carrier was struck off Khasab in the same 24 hours with a crew member missing, and the deal is conditional on Washington lifting a blockade it has not offered to lift.
analysis.bondYieldNote: 5 Aug yields are intraday; the 4 Aug close is confirmed and every trigger runs off it. No channel moved. Score holds at 27/30.

bondYield.title: (i) Treasury — held at 5 (max), and Stage-4 Threshold B has LAPSED.
bondYield.text: This is the move of the edition even though no score changed. The 30Y closed 5.1743% on 4 August and the 10Y 4.6126%, so both legs of Threshold B failed on the same close — the first failure since 28 July and the end of a four-close run that included the 5.2724% and 4.7347% war records of 31 July. This morning’s 5.1806% and 4.6228% leave the threshold unsatisfied on a second session, by 1.94 bp and 2.72 bp. The lapse should be read precisely: it does not repair the long end, which still sits 57.0 bp above its pre-war anchor and 12.43 bp above the 13 May auction stop, and it does not move the channel, which is at its maximum and governed by a downgrade requiring a 30Y close under 5.00% with MOVE under 75. Those legs still fail by 17.43 bp and 2.56 pts. But both have narrowed materially: on Monday they failed by 22.74 bp and 5.48 pts. MOVE closed 77.56, down 2.92 on the session and 5.46 from Friday’s spike, its lowest since 30 July. What makes this the wrong session to conclude anything is the calendar: the quarterly refunding statement lands at 8:30am ET today, hours after this snapshot, against Monday’s $739bn borrowing estimate and 6 May guidance holding coupon sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn ‘for at least the next several quarters’. A long end whose 30Y closed 5.3 bp lower into that statement has pre-positioned for the guidance to survive.

bondYield.title: (ii) Oil — held at 2, and for the first time in the war it is closer to a downgrade than an upgrade.
bondYield.text: The last confirmed close is $77.93 (4 August), $17.07 below the $95 upgrade trigger and $5.45 above the $72.48 downgrade anchor — the narrowest that gap has been since 10 July, and narrower than the $8.61 of Monday. Brent has fallen $10.00 in two sessions from the 31 July close, the largest two-session decline since 6 May, and prints $77.76 this morning in a 71-cent range entirely below Tuesday’s close. WTI’s $74.40 close is likewise the lowest since 10 July. The downgrade requires both legs: a mediated pause AND a close at or below $72.48. The price leg is now within reach on any two sessions like the last two. The pause leg is NOT satisfied and the monitor is explicit about why: a corridor negotiation is not a pause, and a bulk carrier was struck in the strait on the same day the negotiation was confirmed. The physical case for a higher number is also unchanged — effective OPEC+ spare capacity was roughly 0.17 mb/d on the IEA’s July estimate so September’s 188k b/d is a quota rather than a cargo, Jizan’s 400k b/d is out to about 15 August, Abqaiq and Damietta are unreported, and the strait is shut on day 157 — which is precisely the point. The market has repriced the probability of a settlement, not the physical balance. If the corridor deal is signed, this channel can fall to 1 and take the score with it; if it is not, $77.93 with 0.17 mb/d of spare capacity is a fragile price.

bondYield.title: (iii) Escalation risk — held at 5 (max). The downgrade candidate is re-opened, on a different and better-sourced track, and still not taken.
bondYield.text: Yesterday this monitor revoked a downgrade candidate because the negotiation it rested on could not be sourced. Today a negotiation can be sourced, and it is not the same one. Baghaei confirmed on the record that Iran is in bilateral talks with Oman on shipping lanes; Rubio confirmed US involvement in that channel and said there had been progress but ‘not finality yet’; Bessent said a deal to open the strait might come ‘today or tomorrow’. That is the first time in this war that Tehran and Washington have described the same negotiation as existing. It is also, on its face, less than the channel needs. Qatar’s spokesman said no direct US–Iran talks are scheduled; the President’s ‘we are, in fact, talking’ is still contradicted by the mediator and by Tehran; the deal is conditional on lifting a blockade Washington has not offered to lift; and the Minoan Pioneer was struck off Khasab on 4 August with a crew member missing. A stand-down cannot be found in a window that contains a vessel casualty. The correct read is that the downgrade path has moved from ‘unsourceable’ to ‘real but unconsummated’ in one session, and that the channel most likely to move first is maritime, not escalation.

bondYield.title: (iv) US inflation impulse — held at 5 (max), and the forward is the last thing standing.
bondYield.text: 5Y5Y forward inflation closed 2.3180% on 4 August, a sixth consecutive close above the 2.30% trigger and a third consecutive decline from the 2.3597% war record. It has given back 4.17 bp in total. Set that against what everything else did in the same window: Brent gave back $10.00, and the 10Y breakeven closed 2.2278% — its first close below the 2.2569% pre-war anchor since 28 July, having given back 5.68 bp from its 31 July high. Spot inflation compensation has fully round-tripped the war premium it built in July; the forward has given back a quarter of it. That divergence is the whole argument for this channel sitting at 5. A market that thought this was an energy shock would have taken the forward down with the crude. The downgrade — 5Y5Y sustained at or below the 2.142% anchor — is 17.6 bp away and not in play, though it is 2.0 bp closer than on Monday. At 5/5 the channel can only subtract, and today it did not.

bondYield.title: (v) Political stress — held at 5 (max), the upgrade reinforced and the corroboration diverging.
bondYield.text: AUTMUSAG has backfilled 3 August at $4.76, a third consecutive confirmed close above the $4.75 trigger after 30 and 31 July. The 4→5 upgrade fired last edition is therefore better evidenced than when it fired, not worse. The series is blank for 4 and 5 August — three of the last five sessions dark — and is flagged rather than carried. The more interesting development is corroborative: the DOE weekly series flagged as missing last edition has backfilled at $4.079 for the week to 3 August, down 1.7 cents from $4.096, matching EIA’s own release to the tenth of a cent, and AAA’s separately published regular-grade national average printed $4.089 on 4 August against $4.099 a week earlier. The corroborating retail series are easing while the scored series holds at its highs — the first such divergence since June. Two things follow. First, the upgrade stands on three confirmed closes and hysteresis requires a sustained reversal past a wider threshold to undo it, so an easing corroborator does not reverse it. Second, the next AUTMUSAG print is now a genuine test rather than a formality. What is not easing is diesel: EIA had on-highway diesel at $5.348 for the week to 3 August, and refining rather than crude remains the binding constraint on the pump — which is why Brent at $77.93 does not disarm this channel.

bondYield.title: (vi) Maritime denial — held at 5 (max), and this is now the channel most likely to move next.
bondYield.text: The strait is closed on day 157 and the traffic data is not close to the downgrade condition on any tracker: Kpler has 106 all-crossings in the week to 2 August against 98 the week before with about 41% route-undetermined; Windward logged 12 identified transits in the 24 hours to 2 August with half of them dark; TankerMap counted 2 tanker transits on 3 August and none at all on 4 August; CBS News reports 45 commercial vessels redirected since the blockade was reinstated. Against a pre-war baseline that different sources put anywhere between 73 and 130 crossings a day, none of these readings is within reach of traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions. What has changed is the instrument. A signed Iran–Oman corridor agreement — inbound via an Iranian-controlled route, outbound via an Omani-controlled route, fees split — is exactly the event that starts that ten-session clock, and two cabinet-level US officials said on 4 August that it may be days or hours away. It is still unsigned, its implementation timeline is unresolved, and it is conditional on the US lifting its port blockade. The channel does not move on an announcement; it moves on ten sessions of verified traffic.

Tuesday’s 5.8 bp rally is the market betting that does not happen.

stage4.title: Threshold B · 30Y above 5.20% with 10Y above 4.65% — NO LONGER SATISFIED.
stage4.text: The run was 29 July 5.2007% / 4.6773%, 30 July 5.2135% / 4.6733%, 31 July 5.2724% / 4.7347% (both war records) and 3 August 5.2274% / 4.6755%. On 4 August both legs failed together for the first time since 28 July: 5.1743% is 2.57 bp below its leg and 4.6126% is 3.74 bp below its own. This morning’s 5.1806% and 4.6228% keep it unsatisfied on a second session. Three qualifications belong with this. First, a persistence threshold that lapses after four closes has done its job — it warned, and the warning has partially unwound; it has not been falsified. Second, the unwind was a risk-premium unwind across every asset in the same session, not a repair of the fiscal arithmetic that armed the threshold: Treasury still needs $68bn more this quarter than it said in May. Third, the threshold can re-arm on a single bad auction, and the auction is next week. The correct reading is that the long end has bought itself a fortnight, not that the test has passed.

stage4.title: Threshold C · MOVE above 130. Far off, and easing for a second session.
stage4.text: The index closed 77.56 on 4 August, down 2.92 and 5.46 below Friday’s 83.02, its lowest since 30 July. For the first time in the war the two Treasury downgrade legs are simultaneously within a fortnight’s ordinary range of each other — but they must be satisfied together, and the 30Y is still 17.43 bp above its own. analysis.crossAsset: The cross-asset signature this session is a single, coherent, one-directional de-risking — and it is the exact mirror of last Friday. Every field in the extract came in below the value published for it yesterday morning except one: Brent $77.93 against $81.92, WTI $74.40 against $78.66, TTF €55.921 against €58.260, the 30Y 5.1743% against 5.2327%, the 10Y 4.6126% against 4.6858%, the 2Y 4.1917% against 4.2519%, 5Y5Y 2.3180% against 2.3376%, MOVE 77.56 against a carried 80.48, DXY 99.858 against 100.011. The single exception is VIX, up 0.64 to 16.50. On 31 July every field came in ABOVE the snapshot and Brent was $1.97 higher; on 4 August every field came in below and Brent was $3.99 lower. Those are the two largest reconciliation gaps this monitor has recorded, four sessions apart, in opposite directions. What that says is not that the snapshot is unreliable in a random way — it is that the US session is now doing all the price discovery, in one direction per day, on headlines that land after Singapore closes. Underneath the move, the routing signature is intact and strengthening: Henry Hub at $2.693 is 12.1% BELOW pre-war and its 4 August close is the lowest since 29 April, while Asia LNG rose to ¥3,440 and TTF fell for a third session. US gas is not participating in this war, which is the clearest evidence available that it remains a Hormuz-routing shock rather than a global-energy shock. The reading to take is that the market has priced a strait reopening it has not yet been shown.

channels.name: Maritime denial
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max) — and now the channel most likely to move next. Strait closed to commercial traffic, day 157. Kpler has 106 all-crossings in the week to 2 Aug against 98 the week before (+8%), ~41% route-undetermined; Windward logged 12 identified transits in the 24h to 2 Aug, 6 dark, and 312 GPS-jammed vessels in the Gulf; TankerMap counted 2 tanker transits on 3 Aug and ZERO on 4 Aug; CBS reports 45 vessels redirected since the blockade was reinstated. Iran and Oman confirm a live corridor negotiation and two US cabinet officials say a deal may be days away — but nothing is signed.
channels.downgrade: verified reopening (escorted convoys) with traffic above 25% of normal for 10 sessions → to 3–4. A signed Iran–Oman corridor agreement starts that clock; the 4 Aug statements do not.

channels.name: Oil price shock
channels.rationale: Held at 2 — the only channel that can raise the score, and now closer to falling than rising. Last confirmed close $77.93 (4 Aug), $17.07 below the $95 trigger and $5.45 above the $72.48 anchor, the narrowest since 10 Jul; intraday $77.76 in a 71-cent range entirely below Tuesday’s close. Brent has fallen $10.00 in two sessions, the largest such fall since 6 May. Physical supply unchanged: effective spare capacity ~0.17 mb/d, Jizan out to ~15 Aug, Abqaiq and Damietta unreported.
channels.downgrade: mediated pause + close at/below the $72.48 anchor → to 1. The price leg is within reach; the pause leg is NOT met — a corridor negotiation is not a pause and a vessel was struck on 4 Aug.

channels.name: US inflation impulse
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max). 5Y5Y closed 2.3180% on 4 Aug, a SIXTH consecutive close above the 2.30% trigger and a third consecutive decline from the 2.3597% war record — but it has given back only 4.17 bp while Brent gave back $10.00 and the 10Y breakeven closed 2.2278%, its first close BELOW the 2.2569% pre-war anchor since 28 Jul. Spot compensation has round-tripped the war premium; the forward has not.
channels.downgrade: 5Y5Y sustained at/below the 2.142% pre-war anchor → to 4 (17.60 bp away on the last close, 2.0 bp closer than Monday).

channels.name: Treasury stress
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max) — but Stage-4 Threshold B has LAPSED. The 30Y closed 5.1743% and the 10Y 4.6126% on 4 Aug, failing both legs together for the first time since 28 Jul and ending a four-close run that included two war records. The 30Y is 12.43 bp above the 13 May auction stop, down from 17.74 bp. MOVE fell 2.92 to 77.56, its lowest since 30 Jul. The refunding statement lands 8:30am ET today against Monday’s $739bn borrowing estimate; the 30Y leg auctions the week of 10 Aug.
channels.downgrade: 30Y close under 5.00% with MOVE under 75 sustained → to 4. Both legs still fail, by 17.43 bp and 2.56 pts — narrowed from 22.74 bp and 5.48 pts on Monday.

channels.name: Political stress
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max), and the upgrade is reinforced. AUTMUSAG has BACKFILLED 3 Aug at $4.76 — a third consecutive confirmed close above the $4.75 trigger after 30 and 31 Jul. Blank 4 and 5 Aug, flagged not carried. Corroboration is now diverging: the DOE weekly backfilled at $4.079 for the week to 3 Aug, down 1.7c, and AAA’s own regular-grade average printed $4.089 on 4 Aug. Diesel is not easing — EIA on-highway diesel $5.348.
channels.downgrade: sustained retreat toward the $3.52 pre-war level → to 4 then 3. $1.24 above the anchor; hysteresis requires a sustained reversal past a wider threshold.

channels.name: Escalation risk
channels.rationale: Held at 5 (max). The downgrade candidate is RE-OPENED on a different track from the one revoked yesterday, and again not taken. Baghaei confirmed bilateral Iran–Oman talks on shipping lanes; Rubio said there is progress ‘but not finality yet’; Bessent said a deal to open the strait may come ‘today or tomorrow’. Against that: Qatar says no direct US–Iran talks are scheduled, the deal is conditional on the US lifting its port blockade, and the bulk carrier Minoan Pioneer was struck off Khasab on 4 Aug with one crew member missing.
channels.downgrade: mediated stand-down + talks resume → to 4–3. Requires a signed instrument or a convened session, mediator confirmation, and a sustained window with no vessel casualties.

2026-08-05.scoreTotal: CRISIS band — HELD. No channel moved. Five of six channels are maxed and only oil, at 2/5, can raise this number. The composition changed even though the total did not: Stage-4 Threshold B lapsed, the oil downgrade anchor came within $5.45, and a corridor negotiation both sides confirm became the first credible route to a maritime downgrade. For the first time in the war the balance of risks around this score is tilted DOWN rather than up — conditional entirely on an unsigned agreement.

whatsChanged.title: 4 · What's changed since the last edition (4 Aug AM → 5 Aug AM)
items: Score holds at 27/30; no channel moved. Stage-4 Threshold B lapses. Brent falls $10.00 in two sessions. Iran confirms an Oman corridor negotiation. A bulk carrier is struck off Khasab. Source: Bloomberg unless stated.

Stage-4 Threshold B is no longer satisfied, after four consecutive closes including two war records. The 30Y closed 5.1743% and the 10Y 4.6126% on 4 August, failing both legs of the 30Y-above-5.20%-with-10Y-above-4.65% test together for the first time since 28 July. The run it ends was 29 July 5.2007% / 4.6773%, 30 July 5.2135% / 4.6733%, 31 July 5.2724% / 4.7347% and 3 August 5.2274% / 4.6755%. This morning’s 5.1806% and 4.6228% keep it unsatisfied on a second session. The Treasury channel does not move — it is at its maximum and its downgrade needs a 30Y close under 5.00% with MOVE under 75, which still fail by 17.43 bp and 2.56 pts. Source: Bloomberg.

Brent fell $10.00 in two sessions to its lowest close since 10 July, and the oil downgrade anchor is now $5.45 away. The 4 August close of $77.93 is $3.16 below Monday and $10.00 below Friday’s $87.93 — the largest two-session decline since 6 May. It is $17.07 below the $95 upgrade trigger and $5.45 above the $72.48 downgrade anchor, the narrowest that gap has been since 10 July. WTI’s $74.40 close is likewise the lowest since 10 July. The channel holds at 2 because the downgrade needs a mediated pause as well as the price, and there is no pause. Source: Bloomberg.

Iran publicly confirmed a negotiation for the first time in this war — with Oman, not with Washington. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on 4 August that Tehran is in bilateral talks with Oman on establishing safe inbound and outbound shipping lanes, respecting Iranian sovereignty and both states’ security needs, and that results would be announced only once concluded. AP and CBS News report the architecture as inbound via an Iranian-controlled route and outbound via an Omani-controlled route with security and environmental fees split, broad outlines agreed, implementation timeline unresolved, and the whole conditional on Washington lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Secretary of State Rubio said there had been ‘progress made in those talks, but not finality yet’. Source: AP / CBS News / ABC News / Al Jazeera.

Two US cabinet officials publicly forecast a strait deal within days, while Qatar said no US–Iran talks are scheduled. Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC on 4 August: ‘There is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait,’ and on tolls, ‘I think it would be freedom of movement.’ President Trump said ‘we are, in fact, talking’ and attributed his cancellation of the strike package to pressure from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said the same day that no direct US–Iran talks are currently scheduled and that Qatar, Oman and Pakistan are working jointly to create appropriate conditions. Washington is talking up a deal it is not formally party to. Source: CNBC via AP / ABC News / CBS News.

A bulk carrier was struck in the strait, with one crew member missing. The Liberian-flagged, Greek-owned Minoan Pioneer was struck by an unidentified projectile about 20 nm north-east of Khasab, Oman on 4 August, suffering a complete electrical blackout and a fire in the accommodation block; one crew member is missing and the cause is unattributed. Separately the Indian vessel MSV Faize Noore Oliya sank after a projectile strike near Yemen with all 14 crew rescued, and the Houthis claimed a drone strike on Najran airport in Saudi Arabia, which Aramco’s chief executive said had no material impact on production. This is why the escalation channel is not downgraded on a negotiation. Source: CBS News / AP / Splash247 / Riviera Maritime.

Tuesday’s reconciliation was the largest DOWNSIDE gap the monitor has recorded — the mirror of 31 July. Every field in the extract came in below the intraday value published for it yesterday except one. Brent $77.93 against $81.92 (−$3.99); WTI $74.40 vs $78.66; TTF €55.921 vs €58.260; 30Y 5.1743% vs 5.2327% (−5.84 bp); 10Y 4.6126% vs 4.6858% (−7.32 bp); 2Y 4.1917% vs 4.2519% (−6.02 bp); 5Y5Y 2.3180% vs 2.3376%; BE10 2.2278% vs 2.2603%; DXY 99.858 vs 100.011; MOVE an actual 77.56 against a carried 80.48. The exception is VIX, an actual 16.50 against a carried 15.86. Four sessions ago every field came in ABOVE the snapshot. Source: Bloomberg.

The DOE gasoline weekly backfilled and turned DOWN, while the scored series backfilled a third close above its trigger. AUTMUSAG has backfilled 3 August at $4.76 — a third consecutive confirmed close above the $4.75 political trigger, reinforcing the 4→5 upgrade fired last edition. USRFRUSA has backfilled the week to 3 August at $4.079, down 1.7 cents from $4.096, and it matches EIA’s own Gasoline and Diesel Fuel Update released 4 August to the tenth of a cent. AAA’s separately published regular-grade national average printed $4.089 on 4 August against $4.099 a week earlier. The corroborating series are easing while the scored series holds — the first divergence since June. Source: Bloomberg / EIA / AAA.

Correction: the 4 August edition mis-read a narrow snapshot range as a quiet session. The session was violent. That edition wrote that Brent’s ‘very narrow intraday range of 74 cents’ showed the market had ‘stopped trading headlines’. The full 4 August session ran a $6.13 range, from $83.35 to $77.22, the second-widest of the last fortnight after 31 July’s $6.74, and closed $3.99 below the snapshot. The snapshot range measures the Singapore morning and carries no information about the US session. That inference is withdrawn. Source: Bloomberg.

Correction: the strike-planning story was Tier 1 from the start, and the crediting in the last two editions was wrong. The 3 August edition carried US/Israeli planning against Iranian civilian energy infrastructure as a single-outlet Al Jazeera item, and the 4 August edition credited CBS News with corroborating it. Re-verification finds the story originated with Axios (Barak Ravid) on 31 July, reporting that Trump was considering strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure including power plants and bridges within days, sourced to a US official and to Trump’s own cabinet remarks; the Wall Street Journal reported the same day that an attack had been ordered for that weekend. Al Jazeera’s 1 August piece explicitly attributed the claim to ‘major US media outlets’ and was derivative. The correct status is: Tier 1 from the outset, and SHELVED on 2 August when Trump cancelled the package — not disavowed. No Tier 1 outlet has reported its revival and no US official has denied it. Source: Axios / WSJ / Al Jazeera / Washington Post / NBC News.

Correction: the Iraqi militia deadline is NOT corroborated above Tier 3, and there is one date, not two. The 4 August edition promoted this item, citing Rudaw for a 7 August deadline and Ynetnews for a 6 August Kataib Hezbollah deadline. Re-verification finds the 7 August date originated with Press TV on 29 July — Tier 3 — with regional Tier 2 pickup by Shafaq News, Rudaw and Middle East Monitor on 30 July. No Tier 1 outlet carries either date. The 6 August date could not be re-sourced. The item reverts to Tier 3 origination with Tier 2 pickup, exactly as the 3 August edition had it, and should not be used for anything market-moving. Source: Press TV (Tier 3) / Shafaq / Rudaw / MEMO.

US data on 4 August was soft-to-neutral; the two tests that matter land today, after this snapshot. JOLTS job openings for June were little changed at 7.4 million, with hires 5.3m, quits 3.2m and layoffs 1.8m all unchanged. The June goods and services trade deficit narrowed 5.6% to $73.3bn from a revised $77.6bn. ISM manufacturing for July, released 3 August, printed 55.6 with the prices index at 71.1, its 22nd consecutive monthly increase. The Treasury quarterly refunding statement is due 8:30am ET today and the EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report at 10:30am ET — the first EIA weekly since the 24 July print, which had SPR at 307.7 mb after a 3.7 mb draw. Neither is in this edition. Source: BLS / BEA / ISM / US Treasury / EIA.

scenarios.name: Return to full war
scenarios.desc: Lower, and for the first time since 30 Jul it is falling rather than rising — though still the modal path. The strike package was cancelled on 2 Aug and no Tier 1 outlet has reported its revival; CENTCOM has issued no strike release since 29 Jul, seven days; and Trump attributed the cancellation to pressure from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Reuters and CBS report the US has expended ‘virtually all’ of its ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, which the Pentagon disputes but which bears on capacity for a sustained campaign.
scenarios.path: Brent $105–140; MOVE above 90; oil to 3–4; score 28–29 (only oil can rise).

scenarios.name: Deal collapse — talks stall on terms
scenarios.desc: Higher, and now the largest non-war line. The Iran–Oman corridor track is real and confirmed by both sides, which is exactly why its failure conditions are now specific rather than hypothetical: it is conditional on Washington lifting its port blockade, which no US official has publicly committed to; Rubio says ‘not finality yet’; Baghaei says results will be announced only once concluded; and the toll question — Bessent’s ‘freedom of movement’ against Iranian fee proposals — is unresolved.
scenarios.path: Brent $88–105; oil back toward 3; Threshold B re-arms; score 28.

scenarios.name: Contained but violent — blockaded stalemate
scenarios.desc: Higher. The strait is shut on day 157 with TankerMap counting zero tanker transits on 4 Aug, a bulk carrier was struck off Khasab with a crew member missing, and the score sits at 27 regardless because five of six channels are pinned at 5. This is the path in which the market’s repricing turns out to have been premature and nothing in the score reflects it.
scenarios.path: Brent $75–90; MOVE 72–82; risk premium $3–12/bbl; score holds 27.

scenarios.name: Mediated pause — the strait reopens
scenarios.desc: Sharply higher, from the 5% low it hit yesterday, on the first negotiating track of this war that both governments confirm. Two US cabinet officials said on 4 Aug a deal could land within days. A signed corridor agreement starts the ten-session maritime clock and would give the oil downgrade its missing leg with the price already $5.45 from the anchor. It remains unsigned, undated and conditional.
scenarios.path: Brent $70–80; MOVE under 75; maritime→3–4 on verified traffic, oil→1, escalation→4; score falls toward 21–23.

scenarios.name: Regional relapse — Gulf energy infrastructure hit
scenarios.desc: Lower. No confirmed strike on Gulf energy infrastructure on 4–5 Aug; Aramco’s chief executive said recent Houthi attacks had no material impact on production capability. The exposure is unchanged rather than removed: Jizan out to about 15 Aug, Abqaiq and Damietta unreported since late July, effective spare capacity ~0.17 mb/d, and a 7 Aug Iraqi militia deadline that remains Tier 3 in origin.
scenarios.path: Brent $150+; emergency policy response; HY spreads above 500 bp; score 29–30.

2026-08-05.scenarioShift: Probability shifts from the 4 Aug edition: mediated pause +6 (5→11), the largest single rise, because a corridor negotiation that both governments confirm replaced one that neither could evidence; full war −7 (40→33) on the cancelled strike package, seven days without a reported strike and Gulf-state pressure on Washington; deal collapse +2 (26→28) and now the largest non-war line, because a real negotiation has real and specific failure conditions; contained-but-violent +1 (16→17) on zero tanker transits and a vessel casualty; regional relapse −2 (13→11) on no confirmed infrastructure strike and Aramco’s statement. Probabilities sum to 100. The balance of this map has tilted toward de-escalation for the first time since 30 July, and it rests entirely on an unsigned agreement.
watchlist: The Treasury quarterly refunding statement, 8:30am ET today — it lands hours after this snapshot. Monday’s estimate put July–September net marketable borrowing at $739bn, $68bn above the 4 May projection of $671bn, with $628bn guided for October–December. The 6 May refunding held coupon sizes at 3Y $58bn / 10Y $42bn / 30Y $25bn and promised no increase ‘for at least the next several quarters.’ Whether that guidance survives a $68bn upgrade is the question, and the 30Y refunding leg auctions in the week of 10 August. Note the positioning: the 30Y closed 5.3 bp lower into the statement and let Stage-4 Threshold B lapse in the process. If the guidance breaks, that lapse reverses quickly.

Whether the Iran–Oman corridor agreement is actually signed — Bessent said ‘today or tomorrow’. This is the single event that could move two channels. A signed instrument starts the maritime downgrade clock (traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions) and supplies the mediated-pause leg the oil downgrade needs, with the price already $5.45 from the $72.48 anchor. What to verify before treating it as real: a signed or published instrument rather than a statement, Omani confirmation, what happens to the US blockade of Iranian ports on which the deal is conditional, and the toll mechanism. An announcement does not move a channel — the 3 August episode is the reference case.

The EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, 10:30am ET today — and the SPR line in particular. This is the first weekly since the 29 July print for the week to 24 July: crude 404.5 mb and about 6% below the five-year average, gasoline 211.3 mb and 7% below, distillate about 10% below, refinery utilisation 97.2%, and SPR 307.7 mb after a 3.7 mb draw. Refinery utilisation at 97.2% with distillate 10% below average is the mechanism that keeps the political channel elevated independent of crude, and it is the reason Brent at $77.93 has not brought the pump down.

AUTMUSAG’s next print, against a corroborating series that has turned down. The scored series has three consecutive closes above $4.75 and has been blank for 4 and 5 August. The DOE weekly backfilled at $4.079 for the week to 3 August, down 1.7 cents, and AAA’s own regular-grade average printed $4.089 on 4 August against $4.099 a week earlier. Hysteresis means an easing corroborator does not reverse the upgrade, but a backfill materially below $4.75 would change the read on how durable the break is. Watch diesel alongside it: EIA had on-highway diesel at $5.348 for the week to 3 August.

July payrolls on 7 August and July CPI on 12 August, into a market still pricing a September HIKE. The FOMC held on 29 July at 3.50–3.75% by 9–3 with all three dissents FOR a hike. Third-party FedWatch aggregators disagree materially — 82.4% on a September hike as of 27 July against 59% on 4 August — and no reading direct from CME Group could be sourced for 3–5 August, so the level is reported as unverified. ADP was due 5 August and ISM services on 6 August. Both payrolls and CPI land before the 15–16 September meeting, and 5Y5Y at 2.3180% says the market does not believe the inflation argument has been won.

The Minoan Pioneer follow-up, the 7 August Iraqi deadline, and three series to re-verify. The missing crew member and any attribution of the Khasab strike are the immediate items; UKMTO’s last published advisory is Update 079 of 2 August and nothing dated 4 or 5 August could be sourced. The 7 August Iraqi Islamic Resistance deadline remains Tier 3 in origin with Tier 2 regional pickup and no Tier 1 corroboration — it is watched, not used. On the data side: JGLA has no 5 August print and is never carried forward; AUTMUSAG and SOFR are blank for 4 and 5 August; MOVE and VIX printed for 4 August but not 5 August.

methodology.scale: Shock-score scale. Six transmission channels (maritime denial, oil, US inflation impulse, Treasury stress, political stress, escalation risk), each 0–5, summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch · 8–14 stress · 15–21 systemic-risk watch · 22–30 crisis. Market channels move only on a confirmed close through a trigger; escalation-risk and maritime denial are event-based. Hysteresis: upgrades fire on a sustained break, downgrades only on a sustained reversal past a wider threshold, deliberately, to avoid whipsawing. This edition tests the rule from the de-escalation side for the first time. Brent fell $10.00 in two sessions and the long end rallied enough to drop Stage-4 Threshold B out of satisfaction, while a negotiation both governments confirm appeared for the first time in the war — and no channel moved, because the oil downgrade needs a pause as well as a price, and the maritime downgrade needs ten sessions of verified traffic rather than a cabinet official’s forecast. The 25–26 June whipsaw and the 3 August announcement that never became an event are the two reference cases, and both point the same way. A one-session repricing is not a regime change.
methodology.scaleCap: Scale cap — binding on five of six channels, and now cutting the other way. Maritime and escalation have been pinned at 5/5 since 10 and 9 July, Treasury since 14 July, US inflation since 31 July and political stress since 4 August. Only oil, at 2/5, retains any upward range — three points in a thirty-point scale. The consequence readers have been asked to hold for a month is that further geopolitical deterioration cannot raise this score. This edition surfaces the mirror image: a genuine de-escalation cannot lower it either, until it has persisted long enough to move an event channel off its maximum. Brent fell $10.00, Threshold B lapsed, and the score did not move a point. A flat 27 should be read as a saturated scale, not as a stable situation — and that now cuts in both directions.

methodology.gasoline: Gasoline series. Political stress is scored on AUTMUSAG (AAA all-grades retail pump; pre-war $3.52, peak $5.18, latest confirmed print $4.76 on 3 August — backfilled in this extract and a third consecutive close above the $4.75 trigger, following $4.76 on 30 and 31 July and exactly $4.75 on 24, 27, 28 and 29 July — with 4 and 5 August blank). USRFRUSA (DOE regular spot; pre-war ~$2.94, peak $4.50, latest $4.079 for the week to 3 August, backfilled and down 1.7 cents) is tracked alongside as corroboration only. Neither series is re-based. A basis note that has become material now that the two are diverging: AUTMUSAG is an ALL-GRADES series and AAA’s own published national average is REGULAR-grade, which printed $4.089 on 4 August. The gap between them is structural and has run the whole history of this monitor — the same gap exists at the pre-war anchor, $3.52 against ~$2.94 — so a reader comparing the scored $4.76 with a press report of $4.09 is comparing different series, not finding an error. The trigger, the anchor and the full history are all set on AUTMUSAG and re-basing would invalidate them. EIA’s on-highway diesel at $5.348 for the week to 3 August is noted separately because the binding constraint on the pump is refining capacity rather than crude, which is why Brent at $77.93 does not disarm this channel.

methodology.intraday: Intraday caveat. The latest dated row is a Singapore-AM snapshot and US hours set the close. This edition and the 31 July one are now the two extremes of that problem, four sessions apart and in opposite directions: on 31 July every field closed ABOVE my snapshot and Brent was $1.97 higher; on 4 August every field but VIX closed BELOW it and Brent was $3.99 lower.
